Waddle Labs — LLM agents for robotics control Skip to content Waddle Labs We are an applied AI lab building LLMs that control robots. AI has advanced quickly, but robots still struggle outside carefully prepared settings. Making a robot useful often takes work specific to one machine, task, or lab. That makes progress difficult to reproduce and extend, and risks concentrating robot intelligence in a few large companies. We believe individuals should be able to adapt robots to their own needs. Our research aims to make that possible. Model Capability. Language models are not perfect at robotics control, but they can learn in context. We have seen Waddle's agents become markedly more reliable over time. How do we preserve what one agent learns and transfer it to another? How do we build a shared memory across agents? Our work draws on and extends research in continual learning. Inference Efficiency. We have shown that language models can solve robotics tasks in real time, on real robots, but latency remains a bottleneck. How can agents become faster with practice? How can we improve their efficiency while preserving the flexibility to adapt to new tasks and environments? Human-robot interaction. Robot intelligence must be built for people. We study how people can give robots tasks, see what they are doing, and correct mistakes. We design interfaces that make it easy and safe for individuals to collaborate with robots. If you are interested in working with us, please email founders@waddlelabs.ai . For early access or other inquiries, please reach us via wave@waddlelabs.ai .

[https://lamb-labs.com/]
Title: Lamb Labs, the World's First MPU

URL Source: https://lamb-labs.com/

Markdown Content:
Lamb Labs is building MPUs (Model Processing Units). We hardcode the entire model, including its weights, into silicon. The model is the chip. This solves the memory-bandwidth bottleneck GPUs face, targeting 20,000+ tokens per second.

[Scroll](https://lamb-labs.com/#what-we-do)
What We Do

## T he S oftware A nd T he C hip

Fast inference is a full-stack problem. We get more useful tokens out of today's GPUs, then carry the same obsession with speed and efficiency down into FPGA fabric and custom silicon.

### The software

Larry is our one-bit version of Qwen3.8 27B, **14.6× smaller** than the original, so the whole model can fit on-chip. It's the model our first MPU will carry, and you can chat with it live today.

[Larry demo live now ↗](https://larry.trylittlelamb.com/)

### The chip

We turn models into dedicated compute and memory layouts instead of moving every weight through a general-purpose stack. Little Lamb is our smallest end-to-end proof: a model generating text **entirely inside FPGA fabric**.

Little Lamb demo temporarily offline

The road to silicon

## F our S tages

1.   Stage 01 · software shipped

### Larry, a 27B model in one bit

We quantised Qwen3.8 27B to one bit per weight, shaping the model around one hardware constraint: fitting entirely on-chip. Larry is **3.8 GB, 14.6× smaller** than the original weights, and keeps 92% of Qwen's IFEval strict-prompt score. It's the model our first MPU carries. The live demo runs it on a single GPU today.

[Larry demo live now ↗](https://larry.trylittlelamb.com/) 
2.   Stage 02 · shipped

### FPGA accelerator

We compile the model into custom accelerator logic. Our first prototype runs today on an off-the-shelf Kria KV260 board: **an 8B-parameter model under 10 W**, less power than a lightbulb. This board is the proof that the architecture maps to hardware.

[Watch the demo on a Kria KV260 ↗](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/thomas-lanning_getting-the-board-warmed-up-only-6w-to-ugcPost-7484439356724731904-NmGn/) 
3.   Stage 03 · shipped

### Little Lamb, entirely on-chip

We trained a tiny language model from scratch, then burned its weights into FPGA fabric. It generates every token on a **$250 Kria KV260** with all weights resident in on-chip memory and **no DRAM in the token loop**. It is deliberately tiny; the point is a live, end-to-end proof that a self-trained model can run entirely on-chip.

![Image 1: Little Lamb generating text live from a model running entirely inside FPGA fabric](https://lamb-labs.com/little-lamb-live.gif)

**12,000** FPGA token steps/sec**$250** Kria KV260**0** DRAM reads per token

A real prompt, a real reply, and every model weight resident on-chip. The animation above is a screen recording; the live demo is temporarily offline. 
4.   Stage 04 · the endgame

### Custom ASICs

Custom silicon for each model, its architecture hard-coded on-chip. Our target: tape out a chip that runs a 27B-parameter model at **20,000+ tokens per second**. Our RL environment searches chip designs for the best speed and energy per token.
